fields.title: Zechariah
fields.subtitle: Zekharyah, “The LORD remembers”
fields.description: The eleventh and longest of the twelve Minor Prophets, given to the exiles rebuilding Jerusalem after the return from Babylon, beginning in 520 BC. It opens with the call “Return to me, declares the LORD of Armies, and I will return to you”, and eight visions in one night: horsemen among the myrtle trees, a man measuring a city too full for walls, the high priest stripped of filthy clothes before the Accuser, a golden lampstand and the word “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit”. Then it looks far ahead, to a king “humble and riding on a donkey”, a shepherd valued at thirty pieces of silver, a fountain opened for cleansing, “the one they pierced”, and the day when “The LORD will be king over all the earth.” In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Zechariah about?
qa.answer: God’s faithfulness to a small, discouraged people who had returned from exile to a ruined Jerusalem. Chapters 1–8 call them to return to the LORD, encourage them through eight night visions to finish rebuilding the temple, and promise that Jerusalem will be full of life again and that the nations will seek the LORD there. Chapters 9–14 look further ahead, to a humble king who brings peace, a rejected shepherd, the cleansing of God’s people, and the day when the LORD will be king over all the earth.

qa.question: Who wrote Zechariah, and when?
qa.answer: The book names Zechariah son of Berechiah, son of Iddo (1:1), probably a member of a priestly family that returned from Babylon (Nehemiah 12:16). His messages in chapters 1–8 are dated from 520 to 518 BC, in the reign of Darius I of Persia, and Ezra 5:1 and 6:14 name him with Haggai as a prophet of the temple’s rebuilding. Chapters 9–14 are undated and different in style, and many scholars assign them to a later time and author; others hold that Zechariah wrote the whole book. The church has always received it as one book.

qa.question: What are the night visions of Zechariah?
qa.answer: Eight visions seen in one night in early 519 BC (1:7–6:8): horsemen patrolling the earth; four horns and four craftsmen; a man measuring Jerusalem; Joshua the high priest accused and cleansed; a golden lampstand fed by two olive trees; a flying scroll; a woman called Wickedness carried away in a basket; and four chariots going out to the ends of the earth. An angel explains each to the prophet. Together they assure the returned exiles that God has returned to Jerusalem with compassion, will judge the nations that scattered them, will remove their guilt, and will see the temple finished by his Spirit.

qa.question: How does Zechariah point to Jesus?
qa.answer: The Gospels quote it repeatedly in telling of Jesus’s last week. Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a donkey as the king of Zechariah 9:9 (Matthew 21:5; John 12:15). He was betrayed for thirty pieces of silver, which bought a potter’s field (Zechariah 11:12–13; Matthew 27:9–10). He quoted “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will scatter” of his disciples’ flight (13:7; Matthew 26:31), and John saw the piercing of his side as fulfilling “They will look on me, the one they pierced” (12:10; John 19:37). Christians also see him in the Branch of 3:8 and 6:12, who builds the temple of the LORD.

qa.question: Why does Matthew quote Zechariah but name Jeremiah?
qa.answer: Matthew 27:9–10 describes the thirty silver coins and the potter’s field in words close to Zechariah 11:12–13 but introduces them as “the word spoken through the prophet Jeremiah”. A common explanation is that Matthew combines Zechariah’s words with Jeremiah’s accounts of a potter and of a field bought with silver (Jeremiah 18–19; 32), and names the more prominent prophet, as Mark 1:2–3 names Isaiah for a quotation that joins Malachi and Isaiah. Others suggest that Jeremiah stood for the whole collection of the prophets in which Zechariah was read.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
So tell them, “The LORD of Armies says this: Return to me, declares the LORD of Armies, and I will return to you, says the LORD of Armies.”

— Zechariah 1:3

Zechariah is the longest of the twelve Minor Prophets and the strangest. It has horsemen among myrtle trees, a flying scroll thirty feet long, a woman shut in a basket and carried off by women with wings like a stork’s, and a golden lampstand fed by two olive trees. Jerome, who translated it into Latin, counted it among the most obscure books of the Bible. And yet the gospel writers turned to it more than to almost any other prophet when they told the story of Jesus’s last week: the king riding on a donkey, the thirty pieces of silver, the shepherd struck and the sheep scattered, the one they pierced.

The prophet’s name means “the LORD remembers”, and the whole book is a sermon on it. To a small, discouraged people who had come home from exile to a ruined city, it says that God has not forgotten them, or his promises, or the nations.

The prophet and his time

Zechariah was the son of Berechiah and grandson of Iddo, the head of a priestly family that had come back from Babylon (Nehemiah 12:4, 16), so he was probably a priest as well as a prophet. The book of Ezra calls him simply “Zechariah son of Iddo”, and names him with the older prophet Haggai as the two men whose preaching got the temple rebuilt (Ezra 5:1; 6:14).

His first message is dated “In the eighth month of the second year of Darius’s reign”, the autumn of 520 BC, two months after Haggai first spoke. Cyrus of Persia had let the exiles go home eighteen years before, but the city was still largely in ruins and the temple unfinished. The world, as the first vision puts it, was “still and at rest”: Persia was secure, and nothing seemed to be happening to bring about the glorious future the earlier prophets had promised. Zechariah was sent to tell the people that God was at work, and that it was worth building.

Two halves

The book falls into two parts that feel very different. Chapters 1–8 are dated, mostly prose, and tied closely to the years 520–518 BC. They are full of names, Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest, and of the work at hand: rebuilding the temple and the community. Chapters 9–14 are undated, open with poetry and move into visions of the far future. They speak of a coming king, a rejected shepherd, a day when the LORD will be king over all the earth.

Many scholars think that the second half comes from a later time and another hand, and some divide it further; others argue that its differences come from its subject, not its author, and that Zechariah himself, older now, wrote it. Christians have held both views. Either way, the two halves share a great deal: the gathering of the scattered, the cleansing of the land, the nations coming to Jerusalem, and the LORD himself living among his people. And the church has always received them as one book.

  • 1:1–6: a call to return.
  • 1:7–6:15: eight visions in one night, and the crowning of the high priest.
  • Chapters 7–8: fasting turned to feasting. A question about fasts, and ten promises for Jerusalem.
  • Chapters 9–11: the first oracle. The coming king, the gathering of the people, and the rejected shepherd.
  • Chapters 12–14: the second oracle. The pierced one, a fountain for cleansing, and the day when the LORD is king.

“Return to me”

Zechariah’s first word sets the tone for everything else. God was angry with their ancestors, who would not listen to the earlier prophets. “Your ancestors, where are they now? And the prophets, do they live forever?” The prophets died; the people who ignored them died; but God’s words caught up with them. The lesson is not despair but invitation: “Return to me, declares the LORD of Armies, and I will return to you.”

Eight visions in one night

Three months later, on the twenty-fourth day of Shebat, Zechariah saw eight visions in one night. In each he asks what he is seeing, and an angel “who talked with me” explains. Read together, they move from heaven’s view of the world to the cleansing of the land and back again.

  • The horsemen among the myrtles (1:7–17). Patrols report that the whole earth is at rest. The angel of the LORD asks, “LORD of Armies, how long will you hold back your compassion from Jerusalem and the cities of Judah”, and the answer comes: “I have returned to Jerusalem with compassion.”
  • Four horns and four craftsmen (1:18–21). The powers that scattered Judah will themselves be thrown down.
  • The man with the measuring line (2:1–13). Jerusalem will be too full for walls, and God himself will be “a wall of fire around her”. Whoever touches his people “touches the pupil of his eye”, and “Many nations will join themselves to the LORD on that day”.
  • Joshua and the Accuser (3:1–10). The high priest stands in filthy clothes, accused, and is cleansed.
  • The lampstand and the olive trees (4:1–14). The temple will be finished, not by might but by God’s Spirit.
  • The flying scroll (5:1–4). God’s curse goes out against theft and false oaths.
  • The woman in the basket (5:5–11). Wickedness is shut in a basket and carried away to Babylon.
  • Four chariots (6:1–8). The winds of heaven go out to the ends of the earth, and God’s spirit is at rest.

Two visions stand at the centre, and each is about one of the community’s two leaders. In the fourth, Joshua the high priest stands before the angel of the LORD, and the Accuser stands at his right side to accuse him. The Accuser is given no words. The LORD rebukes him: “Is this man not a burning stick snatched from the fire?” Then:

The angel said to those who were standing before him, “Remove his filthy clothes.” Then he told Joshua, “See, I have taken your guilt away from you, and I will dress you in fine robes.”

— Zechariah 3:4

Joshua is cleansed not because he is clean but because God has chosen Jerusalem. And the vision looks beyond him to “my servant, the Branch”, and to a day when God “will remove the guilt of that land in a single day”.

In the fifth vision, Zechariah sees a golden lampstand with two olive trees beside it that feed it with oil. The word is for Zerubbabel, who had a mountain of work in front of him and very little to do it with:

Then he told me, “Here is the word of the LORD for Zerubbabel: ‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of Armies. What are you, great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you will become level ground. He will bring out the top stone while people shout, “Grace, grace to it!”‘”

— Zechariah 4:6–7

The hands that laid the foundation would finish it. And to those who looked at the modest work and sneered, God asks a question that has comforted builders ever since: “Who has despised the day of small beginnings?”

After the visions comes an action. Zechariah is told to make a crown from silver and gold brought by exiles from Babylon and set it on Joshua’s head, with a word about the future: “Here is the man whose name is the Branch.” He will build the temple of the LORD, and rule, and “There will be a priest on his throne”. Whether the verse speaks of one figure or of two in harmony, kingship and priesthood, offices kept apart in Israel, stand together. Christians have heard in it the high priest who, as the letter to the Hebrews says, “has taken his seat at the right hand of the throne” (Hebrews 8:1).

Fasting and feasting

Two years later, in 518 BC, a delegation from Bethel came with a practical question. For seventy years they had fasted in the fifth month to mourn the burning of the temple. Now that it was being rebuilt, should they go on? God answers with a question of his own: “did you truly fast for me?” Then he repeats what the earlier prophets had said:

The LORD of Armies says this: Judge with true justice. Show loyal love and compassion to one another. Do not oppress the widow or the orphan, the outsider or the poor. And do not plot evil against one another in your hearts.

— Zechariah 7:9–10

Their ancestors had refused, and made their hearts “as hard as diamond”, and the land had become a wasteland. But chapter 8 turns to promise. Ten times it says “The LORD of Armies says this” or “The LORD says this”, and the promises are among the gentlest in the prophets. God will live in Jerusalem again. Old men and old women will sit in its squares, each with a cane, “And the city squares will be full of boys and girls playing there.” Then the question about fasting is answered: the fasts “will become times of joy and gladness and happy festivals”. And the chapter ends with the nations:

The LORD of Armies says this: In those days ten people from nations of every language will take hold of the edge of a Jew’s robe and say, “Let us go with you, because we have heard that God is with you.”

— Zechariah 8:23

The coming king

The second half of the book opens with the LORD marching down from the north, through Syria, Tyre and the Philistine cities, to camp around his house. Then a king arrives, and he is not what anyone expected:

Rejoice greatly, Daughter Zion! Shout aloud, Daughter Jerusalem! Look, your king is coming to you; righteous and victorious is he, humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.

— Zechariah 9:9

Conquerors rode horses and chariots. This king comes humble, on a donkey, and takes the chariots and war horses away. “He will proclaim peace to the nations; his rule will stretch from sea to sea”. On the Sunday before he died, Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a donkey, and Matthew and John both quote this verse (Matthew 21:5; John 12:15). He was not making a vague gesture. He was claiming to be this king.

The poetry goes on to promise freedom for “you prisoners who have hope”, rain from the LORD instead of lying diviners, and a scattered people whistled home like a flock.

The rejected shepherd

Chapter 11 is one of the hardest passages in the prophets. Zechariah is told to act out the part of a shepherd for “the flock that is marked for slaughter”, whose own shepherds show them no pity. He takes two staffs, named Favor and Union. But the flock loathes him, and when he asks for his wages they weigh out thirty pieces of silver, the price of a slave in the law of Moses (Exodus 21:32). The LORD’s comment is bitter: “Throw it to the potter, that fine price they set on me!” So the prophet throws the silver into the house of the LORD, to the potter, and breaks his staffs.

Matthew saw this fulfilled when Judas threw back the thirty silver coins he had been paid to betray Jesus, and the priests used them to buy a potter’s field (Matthew 27:3–10). Matthew attributes the words to Jeremiah, perhaps because he joins Zechariah’s words to Jeremiah’s accounts of a potter and of a field bought for silver (Jeremiah 18–19; 32).

The one they pierced

The second oracle begins with the nations gathered against Jerusalem and the LORD defending it. Then, at its centre, comes a verse of extraordinary strangeness:

On the house of David and on the people of Jerusalem I will pour out a spirit of grace and of prayer for mercy. They will look on me, the one they pierced, and they will mourn for him as one mourns for an only son, and weep bitterly over him as for a firstborn son.

— Zechariah 12:10

The LORD speaks, and says “They will look on me, the one they pierced”, and then “mourn for him”. The pierced one is somehow both the LORD and another. Jewish interpreters have read the verse in several ways. John, telling how a soldier pierced Jesus’s side, writes: “And another passage of Scripture also says, ‘They will look at the one they pierced.’” (John 19:37). Revelation takes it further: when Christ comes with the clouds, “those who pierced him” will see him (Revelation 1:7).

The mourning is followed at once by cleansing: “On that day a fountain will be opened for the house of David and the people of Jerusalem, to wash away their sin and impurity.” And then the shepherd appears once more, now as one whom the LORD calls “the man who stands next to me”:

Awake, sword, against my shepherd, against the man who stands next to me, declares the LORD of Armies. Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will scatter; I will turn my hand against even the little ones.

— Zechariah 13:7

Jesus quoted these words on the night of his arrest, on the way to the Mount of Olives, when he told his disciples that they would all fall away (Matthew 26:31; Mark 14:27). Yet the chapter ends with a refined people, brought through fire, who call on God and are answered: “I will say, ‘This is my people,’ and they will say, ‘The LORD is my God.’”

The LORD will be king

The last chapter is the most dramatic in the book. The nations attack Jerusalem; the LORD goes out to fight; his feet stand on the Mount of Olives, which splits in two. There is a day “without day or night; and when evening comes, there will be light”; living water flows out from Jerusalem, east and west, “in summer and in winter alike”. And at the centre:

The LORD will be king over all the earth. On that day the LORD will be one, and his name one.

— Zechariah 14:9

Even the nations that attacked the city go up each year to worship the King and keep the Festival of Booths. The bells on the horses are engraved “Holy to the LORD”, the words once engraved on the gold plate of the high priest’s turban (Exodus 28:36); every cooking pot in Jerusalem is as holy as the temple bowls; and there is no longer a trader in the house of the LORD.

Christians read this chapter in different ways. Some expect a literal future fulfilment in the land of Israel, connected with Christ’s return to the Mount of Olives (compare Acts 1:11–12). Others read its pictures as the prophet’s way of describing what the gospel brings and the new creation completes: living water flowing to the nations, worship of the one God by every people, and the whole of life made holy. They agree on its heart: the LORD will be king over all the earth.

How to read Zechariah

Do not try to read Zechariah in one sitting. Take the first eight chapters with Haggai and Ezra 1–6 beside them, and remember the people who first heard them: a few builders on a ruined hill, wondering whether anything they did mattered. Then read chapters 9–14 slowly, with the accounts of Jesus’s last week open alongside: Matthew 21 and 26–27, and John 12 and 19. Much that seems obscure becomes clear when you see who the gospel writers thought it was about.

In the visions, do not worry if every detail is not explained; Zechariah himself kept asking “What are these?” Look for what the angel does explain, and for the direction of travel: from guilt to cleansing, from scattering to gathering, from small beginnings to a world where everything is “Holy to the LORD”.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The poetry of chapters 9–11, and of a few passages elsewhere, is printed one line per line. A few of the translation’s choices are worth knowing.

“The Accuser.” In chapter 3 the Hebrew has “the satan”, with the article, a title meaning the one who brings a charge in court, as in Job 1. The translation renders it “the Accuser”, so that its link with the verb that follows, “to accuse him”, can be heard. Later Scripture uses the word as a name, and Revelation 12:10 speaks of “the one who accused our brothers and sisters”.

“The LORD of Armies.” Zechariah uses this title for God more than fifty times. It renders what older Bibles call “the LORD of hosts”: the LORD who commands the armies of heaven.

“Loyal love.” In 7:9 the Hebrew hesed, the faithful love that keeps covenant, is “loyal love”.

“A trader.” The last word of the book, in 14:21, is literally “Canaanite”. Since the Canaanites of the coast were famous merchants, the word came to mean a trader, and the translation reads it that way. When Jesus drove the traders out of the temple courts, he acted in the spirit of this verse.

Numbering. In Hebrew Bibles the vision of the four horns (1:18–21 in English) begins chapter 2, so the verses of chapter 2 are numbered four higher. References in this edition follow the numbering of English Bibles.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Zechariah 1
fields.body_html:
A call to return to the LORD

In the eighth month of the second year of Darius’s reign, the word of the LORD came to Zechariah the prophet, son of Berechiah, son of Iddo: The LORD was very angry with your ancestors. So tell them, “The LORD of Armies says this: Return to me, declares the LORD of Armies, and I will return to you, says the LORD of Armies.” Do not be like your ancestors, to whom the earlier prophets called out, “The LORD of Armies says this: Turn back from your evil ways and your evil deeds.” But they would not listen or pay attention to me, declares the LORD. Your ancestors, where are they now? And the prophets, do they live forever? But my words and my decrees, the ones I commanded my servants the prophets to speak, did they not catch up with your ancestors? Then they repented and said, “The LORD of Armies has dealt with us as our ways and our deeds deserved, just as he planned to do.”

The man among the myrtle trees

On the twenty-fourth day of Shebat, the eleventh month, in the second year of Darius’s reign, the word of the LORD came to Zechariah the prophet, son of Berechiah, son of Iddo: I saw a vision in the night: there was a man mounted on a red horse. He stood among the myrtle trees in the ravine, and behind him were red, sorrel and white horses. I asked, “What are these, my lord?” The angel who talked with me answered, “I will show you what they are.” Then the man standing among the myrtle trees explained, “These are the ones the LORD has sent to patrol the earth.” They reported to the angel of the LORD, who stood among the myrtle trees: “We have patrolled the whole earth, and all of it is still and at rest.” Then the angel of the LORD said, “LORD of Armies, how long will you hold back your compassion from Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, which you have been angry with these seventy years?” And the LORD answered the angel who talked with me with good and comforting words. Then the angel who talked with me said to me, “Proclaim this: ‘The LORD of Armies says this: I am deeply jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion. And I am very angry with the nations that feel so secure. I was only a little angry with my people, but they made the disaster worse. Therefore the LORD says this: I have returned to Jerusalem with compassion. My house will be rebuilt in it, declares the LORD of Armies, and a measuring line will be stretched out over Jerusalem.’ Proclaim this as well: ‘The LORD of Armies says this: My cities will once again overflow with prosperity, and the LORD will again comfort Zion and again choose Jerusalem.’”

Then I looked up, and I saw four horns. I asked the angel who talked with me what they were. He answered, “These are the horns that scattered Judah, Israel and Jerusalem.” Then the LORD showed me four craftsmen.

Four horns and four craftsmen

I asked, “What are these coming to do?” He said, “Those are the horns that scattered Judah so completely that no one could raise their head. But these craftsmen have come to terrify them, to throw down the horns of the nations that raised their horns against the land of Judah to scatter its people.”

fields.title: Zechariah 2
fields.body_html:
A man with a measuring line

Then I looked up, and there was a man with a measuring line in his hand. I asked, “Where are you going?” He answered, “To measure Jerusalem, to find out how wide and how long it is.” Then the angel who talked with me stepped forward, and another angel came out to meet him. He said to him, “Run, tell that young man: ‘Jerusalem will be inhabited like villages without walls, because of the great number of people and animals in it. And I myself will be a wall of fire around her, declares the LORD, and I will be the glory within her.’”

Come home from the land of the north

Come! Come! Flee from the land in the north, declares the LORD,
for like the four winds of heaven I have scattered you, declares the LORD.
Come, Zion!
Escape, you who live in Daughter Babylon!

For the LORD of Armies says this, for the sake of his glory he has sent me against the nations that plundered you:
whoever touches you touches the pupil of his eye.
I am about to raise my hand against them, and they will be plundered by their own slaves.
Then you will know that the LORD of Armies has sent me.

Sing and rejoice, Daughter Zion

Sing and rejoice, Daughter Zion,
for I am coming to live among you, declares the LORD.
Many nations will join themselves to the LORD on that day and will become my people.
I will live among you, and you will know that the LORD of Armies has sent me to you.
The LORD will possess Judah as his share in the holy land,
and he will once again choose Jerusalem.
Be silent before the LORD, all people,
for he has risen up from his holy dwelling.

fields.title: Zechariah 3
fields.body_html:
Clean clothes for Joshua the high priest

Then he showed me Joshua the high priest. He stood before the angel of the LORD, and the Accuser stood at his right side to accuse him. The LORD said to the Accuser, “May the LORD rebuke you, Accuser! May the LORD, who has chosen Jerusalem, rebuke you! Is this man not a burning stick snatched from the fire?” Joshua was dressed in filthy clothes as he stood before the angel. The angel said to those who were standing before him, “Remove his filthy clothes.” Then he told Joshua, “See, I have taken your guilt away from you, and I will dress you in fine robes.” Then I said, “Let them place a clean turban on his head.” They placed the clean turban on his head and dressed him in clothes, while the angel of the LORD stood by. Then the angel of the LORD gave Joshua this solemn charge: “The LORD of Armies says this: If you walk in my ways and carry out the duties I give you, then you will govern my house and take care of my courts, and I will give you a place among those who stand here. Listen, Joshua the high priest, you and your fellow priests who sit before you, for these men are a sign: I am about to bring my servant, the Branch. Look at the stone I have placed before Joshua. That one stone has seven eyes. I am going to engrave an inscription on it, declares the LORD of Armies, and I will remove the guilt of that land in a single day. On that day, declares the LORD of Armies, each of you will invite your neighbor to come and sit under your vine and your fig tree.”

fields.title: Zechariah 4
fields.body_html:
The gold lampstand and the two olive trees

Then the angel who talked with me came back and woke me, as someone is woken from sleep. He asked me, “What do you see?” I answered, “I see a lampstand made entirely of gold, with a bowl at the top. There are seven lamps on it, and each of the lamps at the top has seven spouts. And there are two olive trees beside it, one on the right of the bowl and one on its left.” I asked the angel who talked with me, “My lord, what are these?” The angel who talked with me answered, “Do you not know what these are?” “No, my lord,” I replied. Then he told me, “Here is the word of the LORD for Zerubbabel: ‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of Armies. What are you, great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you will become level ground. He will bring out the top stone while people shout, “Grace, grace to it!”‘”

Zerubbabel will finish the house

Then the word of the LORD came to me: Zerubbabel’s hands have laid the foundation of this house, and his hands will bring it to completion. Then you will know that the LORD of Armies has sent me to you. Who has despised the day of small beginnings? People will rejoice when they see the plumb stone in Zerubbabel’s hand. These seven are the eyes of the LORD, which range over the whole earth. Then I asked him, “What are these two olive trees to the right and left of the lampstand?” I asked him again, “What are the two branches of the olive trees beside the two gold pipes that pour out the golden oil?” He said to me, “Do you not know what these are?” “No, my lord,” I answered. So he said, “These are the two anointed ones who stand beside the Lord of all the earth.”

fields.title: Zechariah 5
fields.body_html:
The flying scroll and the woman in the basket

Again I looked up, and I saw a flying scroll. He asked me, “What do you see?” I answered, “A flying scroll, about thirty feet long and about fifteen feet wide.” Then he said to me, “This is the curse that is going out over the whole land. As one side of it says, every thief will be swept away; and as the other side says, everyone who swears falsely will be swept away. I have sent it out, declares the LORD of Armies, and it will go into the thief’s house and the house of anyone who swears falsely by my name. It will stay inside that house and destroy it, timber and stones alike.” Then the angel who talked with me stepped forward and told me, “Look up and see what this is that is coming out.” I asked, “What is it?” He said, “This is an ephah basket coming out.” He added, “This is what they are like throughout the land.” Then the lead cover was lifted, and there was a woman sitting inside the basket. He said, “This is Wickedness.” Then he pushed her back down into the basket and pressed the lead cover down over its opening.

Then I looked up, and there were two women coming out, with the wind in their wings. They had wings like a stork’s wings, and they lifted the basket up between earth and sky. I asked the angel who talked with me, “Where are they taking the basket?” He answered, “To the land of Shinar, to build a house for it. When the house is ready, the basket will be set down there on its base.”

fields.title: Zechariah 6
fields.body_html:
Four chariots

Again I looked up, and I saw four chariots coming out from between two mountains, and the mountains were made of bronze. The first chariot had red horses, the second black horses, the third white horses, and the fourth dappled horses, powerful ones. I asked the angel who talked with me, “My lord, what are these?” The angel answered me, “These are the four winds of heaven, going out after presenting themselves before the Lord of all the earth. The chariot pulled by the black horses is heading for the land of the north, the white horses have gone out after them, and the dappled horses have gone toward the land of the south.” When the powerful horses came out, they were eager to set off and patrol the earth. He said, “Go, patrol the earth!” So they patrolled the earth. Then he called out to me, “Look, those going toward the land of the north have given my spirit rest in the land of the north.”

A crown and the Branch

Then the word of the LORD came to me: Take a gift from the exiles Heldai, Tobiah and Jedaiah, who have just come from Babylon, and on that same day go to the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah. Take the silver and gold and make a crown, and set it on the head of Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest. Say to him, “The LORD of Armies says this: Here is the man whose name is the Branch. He will branch out from his place, and he will build the temple of the LORD. It is he who will build the temple of the LORD, and he will be clothed with majesty, and he will sit and rule on his throne. There will be a priest on his throne, and the two of them will be in peaceful agreement.” The crown will be kept in the temple of the LORD as a memorial to Helem, Tobiah, Jedaiah and Hen son of Zephaniah. People who are far away will come and help build the temple of the LORD. Then you will know that the LORD of Armies has sent me to you. All this will come about if you carefully obey the LORD your God.

fields.title: Zechariah 7
fields.body_html:
A question about fasting

In the fourth year of King Darius’s reign, the word of the LORD came to Zechariah. It was the fourth day of Kislev, the ninth month. The people of Bethel had sent Sharezer and Regem-melech and their men to seek the favor of the LORD, and to ask the priests of the house of the LORD of Armies and the prophets, “Should I go on weeping and fasting in the fifth month, as I have done for so many years?”

Then the word of the LORD of Armies came to me: Say to all the people of the land and to the priests: “When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and the seventh months for these seventy years, did you truly fast for me? And when you eat and drink, are you not eating and drinking for yourselves? Are these not the very words that the LORD proclaimed through the earlier prophets, when Jerusalem was inhabited and prosperous, along with the towns around it, and when people lived in the Negev and the Shephelah?”

Judge with true justice

Then the word of the LORD came to Zechariah: The LORD of Armies says this: Judge with true justice. Show loyal love and compassion to one another. Do not oppress the widow or the orphan, the outsider or the poor. And do not plot evil against one another in your hearts. But they refused to pay attention. They turned their shoulders away stubbornly and stopped up their ears so that they would not hear. They made their hearts as hard as diamond so that they would not listen to the instruction and the words that the LORD of Armies had sent by his Spirit through the earlier prophets. So great wrath came from the LORD of Armies. Just as he called and they would not listen, so they called and I would not listen, says the LORD of Armies. I scattered them like a whirlwind among all the nations they had not known. The land they left behind was so desolate that no one came or went. They turned the pleasant land into a wasteland.

fields.title: Zechariah 8
fields.body_html:
The LORD returns to Zion

The word of the LORD of Armies came again: The LORD of Armies says this: I am deeply jealous for Zion, and I burn with jealous anger for her sake. The LORD says this: I have returned to Zion, and I will live in the midst of Jerusalem. Jerusalem will be called the Faithful City, and the mountain of the LORD of Armies will be called the Holy Mountain.

The LORD of Armies says this: Once again old men and old women will sit in the squares of Jerusalem, each with a cane in hand because of their great age. And the city squares will be full of boys and girls playing there.

The LORD of Armies says this: It may seem too wonderful to the remnant of this people in those days, but will it seem too wonderful to me? declares the LORD of Armies.

The LORD of Armies says this: I am going to save my people from the lands of the east and from the lands of the west. I will bring them back to live in Jerusalem. They will be my people, and I will be their God, bound to them in faithfulness and righteousness.

Let your hands be strong

The LORD of Armies says this: Be strong, you who in these days have been hearing these words from the mouths of the prophets, who spoke when the foundation of the house of the LORD of Armies was laid so that the temple could be rebuilt. For before that time there were no wages for people or for animals. No one could go out or come in safely because of the enemy, and I had set everyone against their neighbor. But now I will not deal with the remnant of this people as I did in the former days, declares the LORD of Armies. For there will be a sowing of peace: the vine will yield its fruit, the ground will give its crops, and the sky will give its dew. I will give all these things to the remnant of this people as their own. House of Judah and house of Israel, just as you were a curse among the nations, so I will save you, and you will become a blessing. So do not be afraid; let your hands be strong.

For the LORD of Armies says this: When your ancestors made me angry, I resolved to bring disaster on you and did not relent, says the LORD of Armies, so now in these days I have resolved again to do good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah. Do not be afraid. These are the things you must do: Speak the truth to one another. In your courts, give judgments that are true and just and that make for peace. Do not plot evil in your hearts against one another, and do not love false oaths. I hate all these things, declares the LORD.

Fasts will become festivals

Then the word of the LORD of Armies came to me: The LORD of Armies says this: The fasts of the fourth, fifth, seventh and tenth months will become times of joy and gladness and happy festivals for the house of Judah. So love truth and peace.

The nations will seek the LORD

The LORD of Armies says this: Peoples will yet come, the inhabitants of many cities. The people of one city will go to another and say, “Come, let us go at once to seek the favor of the LORD and to seek the LORD of Armies. I am going myself.” Many peoples and powerful nations will come to Jerusalem to seek the LORD of Armies and to seek the favor of the LORD.

The LORD of Armies says this: In those days ten people from nations of every language will take hold of the edge of a Jew’s robe and say, “Let us go with you, because we have heard that God is with you.”

fields.title: Zechariah 9
fields.body_html:
An oracle against Hadrach, Tyre and the Philistines

An oracle. The word of the LORD is against the land of Hadrach,
and Damascus is where it will come to rest;
for the eye of the LORD is on all humankind
and on all the tribes of Israel,
and on Hamath too, which borders it,
and on Tyre and Sidon, wise as they think they are.
Tyre has built herself a fortress;
she has piled up silver like dust,
and gold like mud in the streets.
But look, the Lord will strip her of all she has
and hurl her power down into the sea,
and she will be burned up with fire.
Ashkelon will see it and be afraid; Gaza will twist in pain,
and Ekron too, for what she trusted in has failed.
Gaza will lose her king,
and Ashkelon will be left empty.
A people of mixed birth will settle in Ashdod,
and I will cut down the pride of the Philistines.
I will take the blood out of their mouths and the forbidden food from between their teeth.
Those who are left will belong to our God;
they will become one of the clans of Judah,
and Ekron will be like the Jebusites.
I will camp around my house to guard it from those who march back and forth.
No oppressor will overrun them again,
for now I am watching with my own eyes.

Your king is coming

Rejoice greatly, Daughter Zion! Shout aloud, Daughter Jerusalem!
Look, your king is coming to you;
righteous and victorious is he,
humble and riding on a donkey,
on a colt, the foal of a donkey.
I will take away the chariots from Ephraim and the war horses from Jerusalem,
and the battle bow will be broken.
He will proclaim peace to the nations;
his rule will stretch from sea to sea,
from the River to the far ends of the earth.
As for you, because of the blood of your covenant,
I will set your prisoners free from the waterless pit.
Come back to the stronghold,
you prisoners who have hope!
Even today I announce
that I will give back to you double.
For I will bend Judah as my bow and set Ephraim on it as my arrow.
I will rouse your sons, Zion,
against your sons, Greece,
and make you like a warrior’s sword.
Then the LORD will appear above them,
and his arrow will flash out like lightning.
The Lord GOD will sound the ram’s horn
and march out in the storm winds from the south.
The LORD of Armies will shield them.
They will devour and trample the sling stones;
they will drink and roar as if with wine.
They will be filled like a sacrificial bowl,
drenched like the corners of the altar.
On that day the LORD their God will save them, for they are his people, his flock.
Like jewels in a crown
they will sparkle over his land.
How good and how lovely they will be!
The young men will flourish on grain,
and the young women on new wine.

fields.title: Zechariah 10
fields.body_html:
Ask the LORD for rain

Ask the LORD for rain in the season of the spring rain.
It is the LORD who makes the storm clouds;
he gives them showers of rain
and green plants in the field for everyone.
For the household gods speak deceit, and the diviners see lies;
they tell dreams that are false
and give comfort that is empty.
So the people wander off like sheep;
they suffer because they have no shepherd.

The LORD cares for his flock

My anger blazes against the shepherds,
and I will punish those who lead the flock;
for the LORD of Armies cares for his flock, the house of Judah,
and will make them like his proud war horse in battle.
From Judah will come the cornerstone, from Judah the tent peg,
from Judah the battle bow;
from Judah every ruler will come.
They will be like warriors in battle, trampling the enemy into the mud of the streets.
They will fight,
since the LORD is with them,
and the horsemen will be put to shame.
I will make the house of Judah strong and save the house of Joseph.
I will bring them back, because I have compassion on them,
and it will be as if I had never cast them off.
I am the LORD their God, and I will answer them.
The people of Ephraim will be like warriors,
and their hearts will be glad as if with wine.
Their children will see it and be glad;
their hearts will rejoice in the LORD.
I will whistle for them and gather them in, because I have set them free,
and they will be as many as they were before.
Though I scatter them among the peoples like seed,
in faraway lands they will remember me;
they and their children will live, and they will come back.
I will bring them home from the land of Egypt
and gather them from Assyria.
I will bring them to the land of Gilead and to Lebanon,
until there is no room left for them.
He will cross the sea of distress
and strike down its waves,
and the Nile will dry up to its depths.
Assyria’s pride will be brought low,
and Egypt’s scepter will pass away.
I will give them strength in the LORD,
and they will walk in his name,
declares the LORD.

fields.title: Zechariah 11
fields.body_html:
Open your gates, Lebanon

Open your gates, Lebanon,
so that fire may devour your cedars!
Wail, you junipers, for the cedar has fallen;
the mighty trees are ruined!
Wail, you oaks of Bashan,
for the dense forest has been cut down!
Hear the shepherds wail,
for their splendor is ruined!
Hear the young lions roar,
for the Jordan’s thickets are laid waste!

The flock marked for slaughter

The LORD my God says this: “Shepherd the flock that is marked for slaughter, whose buyers slaughter them and go unpunished. Those who sell them say, ‘Praise the LORD, I am rich!’ And their own shepherds show them no pity. For I will no longer pity the people who live in the land, declares the LORD. I am about to hand everyone over to their neighbor and to their king. They will crush the land, and I will not rescue anyone from their power.” So I became shepherd of the flock marked for slaughter, the most afflicted of the flock. I took two staffs; one I named Favor and the other Union, and I shepherded the flock. In one month I got rid of the three shepherds. Then I lost patience with the flock, and they, for their part, loathed me. Then I said, “I will not be your shepherd. Let the dying die and the perishing perish, and let those that are left eat one another’s flesh.” Then I took my staff named Favor and broke it, to annul the covenant I had made with all the peoples. It was broken on that day, and the afflicted of the flock who were watching me understood that this was a word from the LORD. Then I said to them, “If you think it right, give me my pay; but if not, keep it.” So they weighed out my pay: thirty pieces of silver. Then the LORD said to me, “Throw it to the potter, that fine price they set on me!” Taking the thirty pieces of silver, I threw them into the house of the LORD, to the potter. Then I broke my second staff, Union, to break the bond of brotherhood between Judah and Israel.

The equipment of a foolish shepherd

Then the LORD said to me, “Take once more the equipment of a foolish shepherd. For I am about to raise up a shepherd in the land who will not care for the perishing, or look for the young, or heal the injured, or feed the healthy, but will eat the meat of the fat sheep and tear off their hooves.”

Woe to the worthless shepherd

Woe to the worthless shepherd who deserts the flock!
May the sword strike his arm and his right eye!
Let his arm wither away,
and his right eye go completely blind!

fields.title: Zechariah 12
fields.body_html:
The word of the LORD concerning Israel

An oracle. The word of the LORD concerning Israel. This is what the LORD declares, who stretches out the heavens, lays the foundations of the earth and forms the human spirit within each person:

Jerusalem, a cup that sends the peoples reeling

Look, I am about to make Jerusalem a cup that sends all the surrounding peoples reeling. Judah too will be caught up in the siege against Jerusalem. On that day I will make Jerusalem a heavy stone for all the peoples; everyone who tries to lift it will be badly hurt. And all the nations of the earth will gather against it. On that day, declares the LORD, I will strike all the horses with terror and their riders with madness. I will keep my eyes open over the house of Judah, but I will strike the horses of the peoples with blindness. Then the clans of Judah will say to themselves, “The people of Jerusalem are our strength, through the LORD of Armies, their God.” On that day I will make Judah’s clans like a firepot set in a pile of wood, like a flaming torch among sheaves of grain. They will consume all the surrounding peoples on the right and on the left, while Jerusalem stays secure in its place.

Judah rescued, and Jerusalem in mourning

The LORD will rescue the tents of Judah first, so that the honor of the house of David and of the people of Jerusalem will not be raised above Judah. On that day the LORD will shield the people of Jerusalem. On that day even the feeblest of them will be like David, and David’s house like God, like the angel of the LORD at their head. On that day I will set about destroying every nation that comes against Jerusalem. On the house of David and on the people of Jerusalem I will pour out a spirit of grace and of prayer for mercy. They will look on me, the one they pierced, and they will mourn for him as one mourns for an only son, and weep bitterly over him as for a firstborn son. On that day the mourning in Jerusalem will be as great as the mourning at Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo. The whole land will mourn, each clan on its own: the clan of David’s house on its own, and their wives on their own; the clan of Nathan’s house on its own, and their wives on their own; the clan of Levi’s house on its own, and their wives on their own; the clan of the Shimeites on its own, and their wives on their own; and all the clans that remain, each clan on its own, and their wives on their own.

fields.title: Zechariah 13
fields.body_html:
A fountain to wash away sin

On that day a fountain will be opened for the house of David and the people of Jerusalem, to wash away their sin and impurity. On that day, declares the LORD of Armies, I will wipe out the names of the idols from the land, and no one will remember them any more. The prophets too, and the spirit of impurity, I will remove from the land. If anyone still prophesies, his own father and mother will say to him, “You must not live, because you have spoken lies in the name of the LORD.” And when he prophesies, his own father and mother will run him through. On that day every prophet will be ashamed of the vision he prophesies, and they will not put on a prophet’s hairy cloak to deceive people. Each will say, “I am no prophet. I work the soil; I was sold to a man as a servant when I was young.” And if someone asks him, “Then what are these wounds on your chest?” he will answer, “I got them in the house of my friends.”

Strike the shepherd

Awake, sword, against my shepherd, against the man who stands next to me, declares the LORD of Armies.
Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will scatter;
I will turn my hand against even the little ones.
In the whole land, declares the LORD,
two-thirds will be cut off and die,
but one-third will be left in it.
I will bring this third through the fire;
I will refine them as silver is refined
and test them as one tests gold.
They will call on my name, and I will answer.
I will say, “This is my people,”
and they will say, “The LORD is my God.”

fields.title: Zechariah 14
fields.body_html:
A day of the LORD is coming

Look, a day of the LORD is coming, when the plunder taken from you will be shared out within your walls. I will gather all the nations to make war on Jerusalem. The city will be taken, its houses looted and its women raped. Half of the city will go off into exile, but those who remain will not be cut off from the city. Then the LORD will go out and fight against those nations, as he fights on the day of battle. On that day his feet will stand upon the Mount of Olives, which faces Jerusalem on the east. The Mount of Olives will split in two from east to west, opening a very wide valley, as half of the mountain moves north and the other half south. You will flee through the valley of my mountains, for the valley between the mountains will reach as far as Azal. You will run as you ran from the earthquake during the reign of Uzziah king of Judah. And the LORD my God will come; all the holy ones will be with you. On that day there will be no light; the shining lights will grow dim. It will be a day like no other, a day known to the LORD, without day or night; and when evening comes, there will be light. On that day living water will flow out of Jerusalem, half of it to the eastern sea and half of it to the western sea. It will flow in summer and in winter alike. The LORD will be king over all the earth. On that day the LORD will be one, and his name one. The whole land will become like the Arabah, from Geba to Rimmon south of Jerusalem. But Jerusalem will stand high and remain on its own site, from the Benjamin Gate to the site of the First Gate and on to the Corner Gate, and from the Tower of Hananel as far as the royal winepresses. People will live in it, and it will never again be devoted to destruction. Jerusalem will live in safety. This is the plague with which the LORD will strike all the peoples who made war on Jerusalem: their flesh will rot while they are still on their feet; their eyes will rot in their sockets; their tongues will rot in their mouths. On that day a great panic from the LORD will fall on them. They will seize one another by the hand, and each will raise a hand against the other. Judah too will fight at Jerusalem. Riches from all the nations round about will be collected: gold, silver and clothing in great quantity. A plague like this one will also strike the horses, mules, camels and donkeys, and all the animals that are in those camps. Then all who survive from all the nations that attacked Jerusalem will go up every year to worship the King, the LORD of Armies, and to keep the Festival of Booths. If any of the families of the earth fail to go up to Jerusalem to worship the King, the LORD of Armies, no rain will fall on them. If the people of Egypt do not go up and come, they will have no rain either; the plague will come on them with which the LORD strikes the nations that do not go up to keep the Festival of Booths. This will be the punishment for Egypt, and the punishment for all the nations that do not go up to keep the Festival of Booths. On that day the bells of the horses will bear the words “Holy to the LORD”, and in the house of the LORD the cooking pots will be like the bowls in front of the altar. In Jerusalem and Judah every pot will be holy to the LORD of Armies, and all who offer sacrifices will come and use them to boil their meat. And on that day there will no longer be a trader in the house of the LORD of Armies.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
On that day the bells of the horses will bear the words “Holy to the LORD”, and in the house of the LORD the cooking pots will be like the bowls in front of the altar. In Jerusalem and Judah every pot will be holy to the LORD of Armies, and all who offer sacrifices will come and use them to boil their meat. And on that day there will no longer be a trader in the house of the LORD of Armies.

— Zechariah 14:20–21

Zechariah ends in the kitchen. After the visions and the oracles, the earthquake on the Mount of Olives and the living water flowing east and west, the last picture in the book is of horses’ bells and cooking pots. The words that once were engraved only on the high priest’s turban are now on the harness of the war horses, and the ordinary pots of every household in Jerusalem and Judah are as holy as the bowls before the altar. The line between holy and common has not been erased. It has been pushed out until it covers everything.

It is a fitting end for a book first spoken to a few builders on a ruined hill, worried that their work was too small to matter. Zechariah told them that God remembers, that the temple they were building was the start of something that would fill the world, and that one day there would be nothing in it that was not his.

The question the book leaves with you

The book’s first question was put to the people of 520 BC: will you return? “Return to me, declares the LORD of Armies, and I will return to you.” Its last chapters ask a second question, sharper and more personal: what will you do with the king when he comes? He comes humble, on a donkey. He comes as a shepherd and is valued at thirty pieces of silver. He is struck, and his sheep scatter. He is pierced, and those who pierced him look on him and mourn.

Zechariah does not let the reader stand outside that story. The mourning of 12:10 is the mourning of the very people who pierced him, “each clan on its own”, and the fountain of 13:1 is opened for them, “to wash away their sin and impurity”.

Where it points

Few books of the Old Testament are woven so closely into the story of Jesus’s last days. He rides into Jerusalem on a donkey as Zechariah’s king; he speaks of the shepherd struck and the sheep scattered on the way to the Mount of Olives; he is betrayed for thirty pieces of silver; he is pierced on the cross. And the last chapters of the Bible pick up Zechariah’s own last chapter: in Revelation there is no more night, a river of the water of life flows from the throne, and the nations walk by the city’s light. The LORD is king over all the earth.

Where to go from here

A few places in this library to take Zechariah further:

  • On the night visions (1:7–6:8). A. B. Simpson’s sermon Words for Discouraged Workers, which walks through the visions as encouragement for the few builders of the temple; and two chapters of his The Holy Spirit, or Power from on High, “The Holy Spirit in the Days of the Restoration” and “Olive Trees and Golden Lamps”, on Zechariah 4:6.
  • On “Not by might” (4:6). Portraits of Courage – Mary Slessor, an Ochorus Original, whose chapter “Not by Might” takes the verse as its text.
  • On the day of small beginnings (4:10). George Whitefield’s sermon on Zechariah 4:10, preached before the governor and assembly of Georgia in 1770, in Selected Sermons of George Whitefield.
  • On the Accuser and the pupil of his eye (2:8; 3:1–5). Portraits of Courage – Praying Hyde, an Ochorus Original, whose chapter “The Accuser of the Brethren” tells how Zechariah 2:8 stopped John Hyde in the middle of a prayer.
  • Morning and evening readings. Charles H. Spurgeon’s Morning by Morning has readings on the myrtle trees (September 26, 1:8), Joshua the high priest (November 27, 3:1), the one who will build the temple (June 22, 6:13), light at evening time (October 4, 14:7) and the living waters (July 1, 14:8); his Evening by Evening on the comforting answer (February 24, 1:12–13), the four craftsmen (December 5, 1:20), the plummet in Zerubbabel’s hand (November 26, 4:10) and the fallen cedar (September 26, 11:2).
  • On the coming king (9:9). A. B. Simpson’s sermon Personal Responsibility, on Christ’s entry into Jerusalem.
  • On the shepherd struck (13:7). John Henry Newman’s The Shepherd of Our Souls (John 10:11), and A. W. Tozer’s Prepare by Prayer (Matthew 26:31–46).
  • On the fountain and the living water (13:1; 14:8). Horatius Bonar’s Christ the Cleanser (John 13:10), Hudson Taylor’s Unfailing Springs (John 4:14) and William J. Seymour’s River of Living Water (John 4:10).
  • On Zechariah and Christ in the early church. Justin Martyr’s Dialogue with Trypho, chapters 53 (on the king riding a donkey) and 115 (on Zechariah 2:10–3:2); and Augustine’s The City of God, Book XVIII, chapter 35, on Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi.

And read Haggai in this same edition, spoken to the same builders in the same months, and the last week of Jesus’s life in Matthew and John.

Every reference to Zechariah in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather what the great writers of the church have said about each passage. But the best next step may be to return to the book’s promise, spoken first to a city with no walls and no king:

Sing and rejoice, Daughter Zion, for I am coming to live among you, declares the LORD.

— Zechariah 2:10
